transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-09
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 63 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Lena Hart (HelixPath Head ML), Rajiv Menon (Platform Eng), Sofia Ruiz (Data Scientist), Tom Becker (Infra), Asha Patel (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): Deep dive on embeddings/rerank performance and cost for HelixPath. Wanted to balance 95th percentile latency SLO of ~100ms for hero routes while keeping per-embedding unit cost low; discussed vector dims, batching, KV cache reuse, and quantization pathways for on-prem deployment. Next: pilot with 2 models (768 and 1536 dims), cost spreadsheet, and on-prem benchmark runbook.

Transcript (timestamps are approximate; transcription imperfect):
00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Quick roll call?
00:03 Dr. Lena: Lena here.
00:04 Rajiv: Rajiv on the call.
00:06 Sofia: Sofia.
00:07 Tom: Tom Becker.
00:09 Maya: great. Ethan and Diego from my side — Ethan, want to intro?
00:12 Ethan: yeah hi, Ethan Park — SE on inference perf. Today we'll go deep on embeddings + rerank economics. we'll talk dims, batching, kv cache behaviors, and quantization options for your on-prem plan.
00:24 Dr. Lena: top things for us: 95th latency under 100ms for our user-facing rerank endpoint, and cost target of under $X per million embed ops — not public but it's tight. Also privacy: everything must be VPC/on-prem.
00:40 Maya: perfect. quick agenda — perf benchmarks, batching strategies, kv cache, quantization, and ops runbook.
00:48 Ethan: quick baseline — we typically test on A100 and H100. for embeddings we see linear cost with dims but non-linear latency at tails when batch sizes get big and memory pressure kicks in.
01:05 Sofia: can we start with dims? we're trying to decide between 768 and 1536 for our reranker.
01:10 Ethan: right. short answer: 768 is cheaper and lower latency; 1536 usually gives better nearest-neighbor quality for hard biomedical queries, but cost roughly doubles and cache/kv size increases. in our internal tests, 768 hit about 60-70% of top-k recall vs 1536 on our drug-sim dataset.
01:32 Dr. Lena: that's in line with our internal evals. we care about micro gains on recall for safety-critical match. any guidance for hybrid approach?
01:42 Diego: you can do a two-tier approach: generate cheap 768 candidates at high qps and then rerank top N with a heavier 1536 model. that way you keep the user-facing latency low and only pay more for few items.
01:58 Rajiv: that makes sense. what's the numbers on batching? our traffic is spiky — bursts up to 500 qps with steady 50 qps baseline.
02:08 Ethan: batching interacts with latency SLO heavily. for synchronous 95th SLO 100ms, aggressive batching (like 128) will help throughput but blow the tail. recommended starting point for real-time rerank is batch 8-32 with micro-batching and a 20ms dispatch window.
02:31 Tom: micro-batching... what's the overhead at kernel level? we saw some odd stalls with nvlink saturation.
02:37 Ethan: stalls typically happen when KV cache gets big or when you mix different sequence lengths. nvlink issues are infra-specific — Tom we'll want your topology. but at runtime the inference engine uses continuous batching; set a max dispatch delay and prefer prefix caching to reduce per-token work.
02:53 Sofia: can you explain prefix/KV cache behavior for rerank? we're not generating long sequences — it's embed-only then pairwise rerank scoring.
03:01 Diego: for rerank, KV cache is mostly useful if you do autoregressive rerank or if you reuse prefix tokens between queries. for pure embedding models, KV cache size is proportional to sequence len and dims; but more importantly, for rerank where you score multiple candidates, reuse of tokenized context (the query) across candidate scoring can save a lot. we sometimes call it "query prefix reuse".
03:25 Maya: (auto-transcribed: "K V cash") yeah sometimes the auto captions spell it K V cash.
03:29 Rajiv: if we do two-tier with 768 candidate gen then 1536 rerank on top 20, what's the expected latency tail?
03:36 Ethan: ballpark: candidate gen at batch 16 on A100 — median 30-40ms, 95th ~70ms. rerank 1536 scoring top20 with batch 8 (parallel scoring) — median ~40ms, 95th ~110-150ms depending on IO and cache hit. combine with good async composition and you'll be in the 95-200ms range for end-to-end unless you optimize.
04:05 Dr. Lena: 110-150ms is close to our SLO, a bit over. can quantization help cut that?
04:11 Ethan: yes. int8 PTQ gets you ~1.5x speedup and small accuracy drop; int4 is faster but riskier for biomedical domain — accuracy regressions can be non-trivial. we recommend PTQ int8 as first pass, and if you need more speed try QAT or per-channel quant for the problematic layers.
04:34 Sofia: do you have numbers for throughput/cost impact for int8 vs fp16?
04:38 Ethan: rough numbers: int8 can reduce memory by ~2x, latency improves 30-60% depending on kernel availability. cost per inference falls proportionally because you fit higher throughput on same GPU. but depends on whether your runtime has optimized int8 kernels for the target architecture. H100 has really good support; older A100s vary by driver.
04:58 Tom: our on-prem nodes are mixed — a couple H100s and an older A100 box. can Redwood runtime target mixed clusters?
05:06 Diego: yes we support smart routing — you can pin high-precision workloads to H100, and lower-precision to A100. also fallbacks if capacity is low. for on-prem we ship a control plane that runs in your VPC and uses the same routing logic.
05:20 Rajiv: network: will routing between H100 and A100 add extra latency if we go cross-node?
05:24 Ethan: cross-node scoring adds comms; for tight 95th SLO you want to co-locate the worker set or use multi-GPU within a node. NVLink is superior — inter-node over ethernet is slower.
05:36 Dr. Lena: probe: can we do a pilot with both 768 candidates + 1536 rerank and quantized int8 on H100 to measure realistic tails?
05:44 Maya: yes, that was the intended pilot. we'll send pilot config and a harness you can run in your environment.
05:49 Sofia: about caching hits — what hit rate should we expect for our rerank? our user queries are often unique but similar templated context.
05:57 Diego: for templated queries, prefix reuse can get 50-70% hit rates. if queries are truly unique, it's low. we recommend experiment: instrument the tokenization hashes, run a week of traffic to estimate reuse; the pilot harness will include a sim mode to estimate cache hit with your representative payloads.
06:18 Rajiv: can you explain more about batching windows? you said 20ms dispatch window.
06:22 Ethan: yes, set a small dispatch window to accumulate requests up to your target micro-batch; if you set it too long you'll hurt latency. 20ms is a common sweet spot for sub-100ms SLOs, but for ultra low-latency you go 5-10ms and accept lower throughput.
06:37 Tom: do we have any best practices for CPU offload?
06:40 Diego: move tokenization and pre/post processing to CPU threads ahead of the dispatch window. ensure coalescing is done to reduce per-request overhead.
06:48 Sofia: accuracy question — how much drop do you see for rerank quality when going int8?
06:52 Ethan: it depends on model family and domain. for generalist evaluations we saw <1-2% nDCG drop on average for int8 PTQ; for biomedical edge cases it can be 3-5% unless you calibrate. that's why we recommend the two-stage approach and validating on your prompts.
07:10 Dr. Lena: ok. what about vector dims for embedding index size? if we go 1536 our index size doubles roughly — costing storage and more memory for ANN search. any guidance?
07:22 Diego: yes index cost grows linearly with dims. consider product: storage + CPU for ANN search + DRAM for in-memory indexes. sometimes we do compressed indexes (PQ / IVF + PQ) to reduce memory while keeping recall. adjunct approach: use 768 for candidate retrieval and run rerank at 1536 not stored in index — compute on the fly for topK.
07:47 Rajiv: we use Faiss on a CPU cluster; will Redwood integrate well with that?
07:51 Ethan: yes — many customers keep a Faiss or Milvus layer and use Redwood for model scoring. Redwood can also return embeddings via API and you can index externally. For the pilot we can provide connector examples.
08:07 Sofia: let's talk numbers — if we run 100k queries/day with 2-tier approach what's rough daily GPU hours cost?
08:13 Diego: depends on hit rates and rerank fraction. rough back-of-envelope: candidate gen at 768 QPS steady 1.2 — you'd need fractional GPU capacity. rerank on top20 for 10% of queries pushes need up. we'll put exacts in spreadsheet — it's highly config dependent.
08:31 Maya: we'll include a cost-per-million embedded ops table and estimated GPU hours for the pilot config.
08:36 Tom: on-prem network/security: we need to review the control plane design — does Redwood require open egress?
08:42 Diego: for VPC/private deployments the control plane can be customer-managed and run inside your VPC; minimal egress is needed for telemetry if you want it. if fully air-gapped we provide an on-prem package. we'll share SOC2 docs and runbook.
08:58 Rajiv: what's the log retention cost and are embeddings considered PII?
09:02 Maya: log retention is configurable; for regulated data you can disable retention and enable KMS-backed encryption. embeddings may be considered derived data so treat them as sensitive — we recommend policy review.
09:12 Sofia: any mention of fallback model? if H100 is saturated can we drop to a quantized variant?
09:18 Ethan: yes runtime can fallback to a lower-precision model pinned to A100 or CPU for non-critical routes — graceful degradation. it's supported in rollout policies.
09:27 Dr. Lena: what's the instrumentation available to track 95th latency and per-token cost?
09:31 Maya: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and tracing hooks. we'll demo in the next call.
09:39 Rajiv: can you walk through an example config line — batch size vs dispatch window vs max wait?
09:44 Ethan: sample: batch_max=32, dispatch_window_ms=20, max_wait_ms=50, kv_cache_enabled=true, quant_profile=int8_ptq. that typically gives good throughput with sub-100ms tails for medium load.
10:00 Tom: our infra team worried about GPU fragmentation — if we allocate reserved slots for the pilot will that be a huge waste?
10:06 Diego: Redwood Dedicated supports burst and reserved capacity; for pilot reserved small pools and autoscale buffer can limit waste. for on-prem you can carve quotas per service.
10:15 Sofia: can you explain how candidate gen batching differs from rerank scoring batching?
10:19 Ethan: candidate gen is about generating embeddings for queries, usually single-shot so small seq lengths. rerank scoring often involves scoring many candidates per query where you can leverage matrixized scoring (batch the candidate tokens) — so the effective batch size there is queries * candidates, which can explode if not constrained. we recommend shaping rerank to keep per-device batch within kernel sweet spot.
10:42 Rajiv: often we do pairwise cross-encoder rerank which is heavy. any tips to reduce compute?
10:47 Diego: cross-encoder is heavier; alternatives: bi-encoder + asymmetric rerank, hybrid index with lightweight cross-encoder on top-k. distillation is another path: train a smaller model to mimic the big one for rerank.
10:58 Dr. Lena: sounds good. can we talk about pilot deliverables?
11:01 Maya: deliverables: pilot config + cost sheet, microbenchmark harness, sample dataset of 3 prompt sets, and runbook for on-prem deploy + SOC2 pack.
11:09 Sofia: timeline?
11:11 Maya: we'll send config by 2026-03-12, harness week of 3/15, and schedule the on-prem planning meeting week of 3/23.
11:18 Tomas: (mumbled) sounds good.
11:21 Ethan: final quick note on quantization: try int8 PTQ first. if you see >2% quality drop on your biomedical prompts, use selective per-channel q or do QAT on critical layers.
11:35 Dr. Lena: ok, thanks. also we'll share internal recall thresholds for safety checks.
11:38 Maya: perfect. any other questions?
11:42 Rajiv: how do we surface anomalies in quality after rollout? is there eval automation?
11:46 Diego: Redwood Optimize supports prompt sets/evals and regression alerts; it can tie alerts to model rollouts and send slack. we'll include setup guide.
11:56 Sofia: small question — does Redwood support compressed indexes (PQ) out of the box?
12:00 Ethan: we integrate with indexes; compressed vector stores are supported via connectors. we also have recommendations for IVF/PQ params for different dims.
12:10 Tom: regarding security, what's the KMS integration?
12:14 Diego: we integrate with AWS KMS, Hashicorp Vault, and customer HSM via PKCS#11 for enterprise. keys can be customer-managed.
12:24 Maya: ok last step recap: Maya sends pilot spreadsheet and SOC2 docs, Ethan sends harness and sample scripts, HelixPath provides prompt sets + infra topology.
12:32 Dr. Lena: thanks all — looking forward.
12:34 Maya: we'll follow up in email with calendar invites for the planning meeting.
12:38 [meeting end]
